title: Off Broadway Review: DUKE & ROYA - Bored & Confused?
transcript: Hello. Welcome to Bored and Confused, where I review shows based on two criteria. One, was I bored? Two, was I confused. Today's show is Duke and Roya playing off Broadway. Now, before I get into this, please remember to like, comment, and subscribe. It really helps me grow this channel and helps me to get press tickets so I can review more shows. All right, so I came into Duke and Roya knowing absolutely nothing about it. So, let's start with a little background. This play is written by Charles Randolph Wright, who you might know as the director of Mottown the musical. But before Duke and Roya made its off Broadway debut, it existed in a different form. Back in 2013, Randolph Wright premiered a version called Love in Afghanistan at Arena Stage in DC. He was inspired by a real cultural tradition in Afghanistan known as bacha where young girls are raised as boys so they can access education and have mobility. That detail stays in the final version. But now more than a decade later the story's been reshaped with a clear romantic hook and a more marketable title Duke and Roya. So what is Duke and Roya about? Well, Duke is a famous American rapper visiting a military base in Kabul to perform for the US troops. While he's there, he meets Roya, an Afghan interpreter working at the base with her father. There's instant chemistry, banter, a bit of culture clash, and before you know it, he's persuading her to sneak him off base so he can see the real Kabul. What follows is part love story, part political drama, part family soap opera, and part travalogue with some original rap thrown in for good measure. Which brings me to my big question. What kind of play is this? Is it a romantic comedy or is it a sociopolitical drama about war, displacement, and America's history of using and abandoning local allies? The show keeps flip-flopping between these two, and it never quite settles into either genre. It starts feeling like a romance, then suddenly pivots into a war zone thriller, then back to romantic banter, then a sexy reunion in Dubai. And considering the title is Duke and Roya and not Afghanistan the reckoning, I'm guessing the heart of it really is supposed to be a love story. But here's my issue. For me to get behind a love story, I need to want the couple to be together. And in this case, I I just didn't. Duke as a character is very frustrating. He comes off as cocky, performative, and full of swagger. He's all posturing and broy charm until he suddenly drops a roomie quote and we're supposed to think, "Oh, he's deep." And just when I start to like him a little bit because I want to, he does something awful again, like pressuring Roya to sneak him out of a secure military base, risking her job, her safety, and her family's future. Because why? He wants to buy jewelry. And Roya is smart. She's strong. So, I keep asking myself, why is she following for this act? That was my biggest confusion. I didn't understand her choices, and I didn't believe the romance. The whole will they, won't they thing only works if both characters are worth rooting for. And in this case, I felt like I was watching her babysit a manchild while he put everyone in danger. It didn't feel romantic. It felt reckless, and I just couldn't get on board. Also, I was confused by the tone of the play. The play starts with this serious almost poetic quote about America's endless wars. And I thought, okay, we're diving into something heavy. But then we get quirky romcom dialogue between Duke and Roya. Also, the pacing of this show is slow. The first act especially felt like it kind of dragged along. When the first act ended, my friend who I brought along with me looked over at me and was kind of confused. He said, "Is it over?" And it had only been 75 minutes, but it felt much longer. That said, I was not bored. The the show is well directed overall, despite the slow pacing and the slow scene changes. The lighting and the scenic design are top-notch. I like most of the costume design, and the performances are really solid. Stephanie Nur brings real intelligence and dignity to Roya. And Noma Dumiswaney as Duke's mother is a total pro. Every time she came on stage, I perked up. She's like the common sense fairy godmother these characters all so desperately need. But some of the direction did confuse me. Just a tiny example. There's a scene where Roya's father is entertaining Duke's mother in his office and there's a chair available but instead of offering it, he clears a space on his desk for her to sit and she's wearing a skirt. So it just seemed a little like the director wanted to do levels, but I was like, give the poor woman a chair. And Nome is such a good actress that she even made a little moment out of it, like, "Oh, I'm going to sit on the desk." Also, the ending of the play felt a little too easy and it felt kind of rushed, like we just needed to wrap it all up with a bow. And considering how high the stakes had been, war, trauma, international politics, I wanted more than a tidy everything works out moment. It didn't really feel earned. So, but my final thoughts, despite some of my negative critiques, Juke and Roya is worth seeing. There are excellent performances, there are powerful moments, and under all the tonal inconsistency, there is a real attempt to tell a story about connection across cultures, the scars of war, and the emotional cost of Americans foreign policy without being too preachy. So, if you want to check it out, tickets are available on TDF for 35 bucks and Rush tickets are also available for 39 on Today Tix. The play runs through August 24th at the Lucille Lortell Theater. And I think you should go check it out. Thank you for watching and please let me know your thoughts in the comments and don't forget to like and subscribe. Okay, I'll see you at the next one. >> Don't want to drift away. Keep me engaged. Keep me amused with what's in front of me. Cuz I don't want to be bored and confused.
